nodes.body:
1994 Jan 1. RGG; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution
note: There was no date on the original document so 1994 Jan 1 was assigned since most of the SLHs were prepared from 1994 thru 1997.

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Marsh Killifish
Scientific Name:  Fundulus confluentus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Atheriniformes
	Family:  Cyprinodontidae

Other Common Names: Marsh Mummichog

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Goode and Bean 1879).
	Reference for Classification (1914)
	Revision date should be checked

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Possibly sold as bait as "mummichog".  Consumes mosquito larvae readily as natural food source (2366, 2427).
Recreational:  Possibly caught for bait by recreational fisherman.
Ecological:  This is an abundant euryhaline marsh resident of the southeastern United States, which feeds on a variety of marsh invertebrates, though principally mosquito larvae as post larvae and juveniles (664; 2431; 2421; 2366, 2427, 2367; 2365) and is subsequently consumed by piscivorous fishes and birds (2430).  In the Indian River Lagoon and south Florida it is considered a keystone species along with the sheepshead minnow, eastern mosquitofish and sailfin molly.
Indicator:  This species depends solely on fresh or salt water marsh habitat, particularly high marsh habitat through its entire life history.  Its eggs withstand seasonal exposure before marsh flooding (2425).  Apparently this species is dependent on tidal and natural seasonal water fluctuations as marsh impoundment eradicates this species (2367; 2363) and it is most abundant in periodically dry freshwater marshes throughout south Florida (2371).  Therefore, the absence of this species from previously inhabited salt marshes is a good indicator of changes in natural flooding patterns, particularly when associated with marsh impoundment.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Peninsula Florida from the St. Johns River in Duval County on the east coast to Apalachicola Bay on the Gulf coast (2431; 2423).  The marsh killifish intergrades with F. pulvereus both on the northeast Florida coast and west of Apalachicola to Escambia Bay on the Florida west coast (2423).
Within Study Area: In marginal wetlands and particularly unimpounded or tidal high marsh habitats throughout the Indian River Lagoon (2424, 1959b; 2427; Gilmore 1977).
Life Mode:  Juveniles and adults are usually diurnally active in schools over sand bottom in shallow marsh habitats (2427; Kushlan 1973; 2371).  Eggs are benthic while larvae are epibenthic or demersal (2425).
Mobility and Migration: Adults and juveniles make local migrations associated with water level changes, but tend to prefer open shallow flats rather than ponds and deeper creeks (McLane 1955; 2371).  Lack of movement associated with the preference for shallow flats may in fact allow the species to be stranded with water recession (Kushlan 1973).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
Egg: eggs are benthic, laid in sods or algal mats associated with sea-ox-eye, Borrichia frutescens,  sawgrass, Cladium jamaicense, sedge, Fimbristylis castanea and water hysop, Bacopa Monnieri.  Eggs withstand exposure within moist sediment or algae for at least three months between either tidal or rainwater flooding of the wetland (Harrington and Haeger 1958; 2425).
Larvae: larvae hatch after 15 to 30 min of egg immersion and are epibenthic in the same habitat as eggs (2425).
Juvenile: juveniles and adults forage over open bottoms on salt and freshwater marsh flats (sawgrass, cypress or saltwort and mangrove wetlands; Odum and Heald 1972; 2427; Kushlan 1973; 2371), but also occur in tidal creeks and freshwater spring runs (McLane 1955; Gilmore 1987).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body:
Juvenile: juveniles and adults occur over sand, mud, detrital and algal bottoms near emergent wetland vegetation (2425; 2427; 2371).  Typically "... it is most numerous in shallow waters over a pale substrate (2371).
Adult: Same as Juveniles.

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Salinity: This is a euryhaline species occurring in abundance in highly saline barrier island salt marshes to freshwater cypress swamps and the Everglades.  Recorded from salinities of 0.00 - 53.9 ppt.
Temperature: temperatures range 12.0-28.3 C (Gunter and Hall 1963; 2365).  Apparently aerially exposed eggs can survive temperatures below 4.4 C for brief periods (2425).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: The marsh killifish is gonochoristic, polygamous, oviparous, and iteroparous; eggs are fertilized externally (2424, 1959b).
Mating/Spawning: Spawning occurs over shallow marginal bottoms on algal mats throughout the year though most spawning occurs between February and October in the Indian River Lagoon (2424, 2425).  Principal spawning during the Spring and Fall is suggested by experimental observation of optimum mature ova production with short day lengths (7 hrs) in association with high temperatures (30?C)(2425).  Spawning occurs in fresh or saline waters (2424; 2371).
Fecundity: Marsh killifish may produce 34 - 61 ripe ova during one spawning event (2365).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Eggs:  Eggs are demersal, spherical, with chorionic bristles and filaments and 1.6 - 1.8 mm in diameter after fertilization (2421).  Yolk with 10-15 oil globules.  Ovarian/ovulated eggs average diameter of 0.8 to 1.5 mm at maturation.  Incubation of immersed eggs may take 10-28 days (2365).  Eggs withstand exposure within moist sediment or algae for at least three months between annual sea level rise, tidal or rainwater flooding of the wetland (Harrington and Haeger 1958; 2425).
Larvae: larvae hatch after 15 to 30 min of egg immersion and are epibenthic in the same habitat as eggs (2425).  Larvae which hatch from continually immersed eggs differ from larvae which developed in exposed eggs and were secondarily immersed.  Hatching length in continually immersed eggs is 4.0-5.6 mm (2365),  whereas, hatchlings from reimmersed exposed eggs are equal to 2-4 week larvae from water hatched eggs (measurements not given, Harrington 1959).
Juvenile:   Unknown.
Adults:  Maturation occurs at 40 mm TL (2431).  Age is unknown.

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: The feeding habits of larvae are largely unknown, although Harrington and Harrington (1961) found 11-17mm SL fish feeding only on mosquito larvae.  Juveniles (< 40 mm SL) are omnivorous, although crustaceans (copepods, ostracods, cheliferans and amphipods) and insects (mostly larval dipterans) made up the majority of the diet (2366, 2427, 2367).  Plant materials in juveniles consisted mostly of algae (10% of total diet volume; 2427).  Adults are increasingly carnivorous with growth, with fishes, crustaceans and molluscs playing a prominent role in the diet of killifish 70-79 mm SL (2366, 2427).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Predation:  Due to its abundance in freshwater and marine wetlands it is highly likely that the marsh killifish plays an important role as prey for wetland predators, wading birds, cormorants, semi-aquatic reptiles, largemouth bass, snook, tarpon and ladyfish (2430; 2422).
Factors Influencing Populations:  Marsh killifish populations are extirpated with wetland impoundment (2363, 2367).  This species apparently  requires water level fluctuations or some other major environmental or biological parameter for survival (possibly mosquito larvae for early development).  Therefore, the impoundment of 90% of the coastal wetlands along the Indian River Lagoon (2432) has undoubtedly had a significant impact on this species.  Under natural conditions predation probably plays the most significant role in influencing population patterns.

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title:  Marsh Killifish (Fundulus confluentus)

FLELMR Code:  1404

sections.heading: Revisions
sections.content:
1994 Jan 1. RGG; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution
note: There was no date on the original document so 1994 Jan 1 was assigned since most of the SLHs were prepared from 1994 thru 1997.

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Common Name:  Marsh Killifish
Scientific Name:  Fundulus confluentus

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Atheriniformes
	Family:  Cyprinodontidae

Other Common Names: Marsh Mummichog

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Goode and Bean 1879).
	Reference for Classification (1914)
	Revision date should be checked

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Possibly sold as bait as "mummichog".  Consumes mosquito larvae readily as natural food source (2366, 2427).
Recreational:  Possibly caught for bait by recreational fisherman.
Ecological:  This is an abundant euryhaline marsh resident of the southeastern United States, which feeds on a variety of marsh invertebrates, though principally mosquito larvae as post larvae and juveniles (664; 2431; 2421; 2366, 2427, 2367; 2365) and is subsequently consumed by piscivorous fishes and birds (2430).  In the Indian River Lagoon and south Florida it is considered a keystone species along with the sheepshead minnow, eastern mosquitofish and sailfin molly.
Indicator:  This species depends solely on fresh or salt water marsh habitat, particularly high marsh habitat through its entire life history.  Its eggs withstand seasonal exposure before marsh flooding (2425).  Apparently this species is dependent on tidal and natural seasonal water fluctuations as marsh impoundment eradicates this species (2367; 2363) and it is most abundant in periodically dry freshwater marshes throughout south Florida (2371).  Therefore, the absence of this species from previously inhabited salt marshes is a good indicator of changes in natural flooding patterns, particularly when associated with marsh impoundment.

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Peninsula Florida from the St. Johns River in Duval County on the east coast to Apalachicola Bay on the Gulf coast (2431; 2423).  The marsh killifish intergrades with F. pulvereus both on the northeast Florida coast and west of Apalachicola to Escambia Bay on the Florida west coast (2423).
Within Study Area: In marginal wetlands and particularly unimpounded or tidal high marsh habitats throughout the Indian River Lagoon (2424, 1959b; 2427; Gilmore 1977).
Life Mode:  Juveniles and adults are usually diurnally active in schools over sand bottom in shallow marsh habitats (2427; Kushlan 1973; 2371).  Eggs are benthic while larvae are epibenthic or demersal (2425).
Mobility and Migration: Adults and juveniles make local migrations associated with water level changes, but tend to prefer open shallow flats rather than ponds and deeper creeks (McLane 1955; 2371).  Lack of movement associated with the preference for shallow flats may in fact allow the species to be stranded with water recession (Kushlan 1973).

sections.heading: Habitat Type
sections.content:
Egg: eggs are benthic, laid in sods or algal mats associated with sea-ox-eye, Borrichia frutescens,  sawgrass, Cladium jamaicense, sedge, Fimbristylis castanea and water hysop, Bacopa Monnieri.  Eggs withstand exposure within moist sediment or algae for at least three months between either tidal or rainwater flooding of the wetland (Harrington and Haeger 1958; 2425).
Larvae: larvae hatch after 15 to 30 min of egg immersion and are epibenthic in the same habitat as eggs (2425).
Juvenile: juveniles and adults forage over open bottoms on salt and freshwater marsh flats (sawgrass, cypress or saltwort and mangrove wetlands; Odum and Heald 1972; 2427; Kushlan 1973; 2371), but also occur in tidal creeks and freshwater spring runs (McLane 1955; Gilmore 1987).

sections.heading: Substrate
sections.content:
Juvenile: juveniles and adults occur over sand, mud, detrital and algal bottoms near emergent wetland vegetation (2425; 2427; 2371).  Typically "... it is most numerous in shallow waters over a pale substrate (2371).
Adult: Same as Juveniles.

sections.heading: Physical/Chemical
sections.content:
Salinity: This is a euryhaline species occurring in abundance in highly saline barrier island salt marshes to freshwater cypress swamps and the Everglades.  Recorded from salinities of 0.00 - 53.9 ppt.
Temperature: temperatures range 12.0-28.3 C (Gunter and Hall 1963; 2365).  Apparently aerially exposed eggs can survive temperatures below 4.4 C for brief periods (2425).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode: The marsh killifish is gonochoristic, polygamous, oviparous, and iteroparous; eggs are fertilized externally (2424, 1959b).
Mating/Spawning: Spawning occurs over shallow marginal bottoms on algal mats throughout the year though most spawning occurs between February and October in the Indian River Lagoon (2424, 2425).  Principal spawning during the Spring and Fall is suggested by experimental observation of optimum mature ova production with short day lengths (7 hrs) in association with high temperatures (30?C)(2425).  Spawning occurs in fresh or saline waters (2424; 2371).
Fecundity: Marsh killifish may produce 34 - 61 ripe ova during one spawning event (2365).

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Eggs:  Eggs are demersal, spherical, with chorionic bristles and filaments and 1.6 - 1.8 mm in diameter after fertilization (2421).  Yolk with 10-15 oil globules.  Ovarian/ovulated eggs average diameter of 0.8 to 1.5 mm at maturation.  Incubation of immersed eggs may take 10-28 days (2365).  Eggs withstand exposure within moist sediment or algae for at least three months between annual sea level rise, tidal or rainwater flooding of the wetland (Harrington and Haeger 1958; 2425).
Larvae: larvae hatch after 15 to 30 min of egg immersion and are epibenthic in the same habitat as eggs (2425).  Larvae which hatch from continually immersed eggs differ from larvae which developed in exposed eggs and were secondarily immersed.  Hatching length in continually immersed eggs is 4.0-5.6 mm (2365),  whereas, hatchlings from reimmersed exposed eggs are equal to 2-4 week larvae from water hatched eggs (measurements not given, Harrington 1959).
Juvenile:   Unknown.
Adults:  Maturation occurs at 40 mm TL (2431).  Age is unknown.

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: The feeding habits of larvae are largely unknown, although Harrington and Harrington (1961) found 11-17mm SL fish feeding only on mosquito larvae.  Juveniles (< 40 mm SL) are omnivorous, although crustaceans (copepods, ostracods, cheliferans and amphipods) and insects (mostly larval dipterans) made up the majority of the diet (2366, 2427, 2367).  Plant materials in juveniles consisted mostly of algae (10% of total diet volume; 2427).  Adults are increasingly carnivorous with growth, with fishes, crustaceans and molluscs playing a prominent role in the diet of killifish 70-79 mm SL (2366, 2427).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
Predation:  Due to its abundance in freshwater and marine wetlands it is highly likely that the marsh killifish plays an important role as prey for wetland predators, wading birds, cormorants, semi-aquatic reptiles, largemouth bass, snook, tarpon and ladyfish (2430; 2422).
Factors Influencing Populations:  Marsh killifish populations are extirpated with wetland impoundment (2363, 2367).  This species apparently  requires water level fluctuations or some other major environmental or biological parameter for survival (possibly mosquito larvae for early development).  Therefore, the impoundment of 90% of the coastal wetlands along the Indian River Lagoon (2432) has undoubtedly had a significant impact on this species.  Under natural conditions predation probably plays the most significant role in influencing population patterns.
